items.prompt: We are moving our Windows file server, with all its share permissions, to AWS. Can we just use EFS like our Linux team does?
items.ten_second: No. EFS doesn't support Windows instances. FSx for Windows File Server gives you managed SMB shares that join your Active Directory.
sixty_second: The short answer is no. EFS doesn't support Windows instances.
Use FSx for Windows File Server. It's a managed Windows file server with SMB shares.
It works like this. You join the file system to your Active Directory domain.
Your users sign in with their domain accounts, as they do today.
File and folder permissions are normal Windows permissions, so your current ones move with the data.
You copy the files with AWS DataSync, or with Robocopy.
A DNS alias lets people keep the old share name.
The thing to watch is the directory.
FSx joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or your own Active Directory. AD Connector and Simple AD don't work.
In your case, the directory decides the plan.
Where does your Active Directory run today, on premises or in AWS?

key_points.point: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported.
FSx for Windows File Server provides fully managed Windows file servers and supports the SMB protocol.
You join the file system to your Active Directory domain, which gives user authentication and file- and folder-level access control.
accept: users sign in with domain accounts

key_points.point: The file system joins AWS Managed Microsoft AD or a self-managed Active Directory; Amazon FSx does not support AD Connector or Simple AD.

key_points.point: FSx uses standard Windows ACLs, and an existing ACL configuration migrates without modifications; AWS recommends DataSync for the copy, with Robocopy as an alternative.
DNS aliases let users keep the existing DNS names of the shares after the move.

follow_ups.question: What happens if one Availability Zone fails?
follow_ups.answer: Choose a Multi-AZ file system. It fails over to a standby file server in a second zone, typically in less than 30 seconds. A Single-AZ file system usually has about 30 minutes of downtime during recovery.

follow_ups.question: Is there a size limit for one file system?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. One file system holds up to 64 TiB. You can increase its storage capacity later, but you cannot decrease it.

items.prompt: A volume, a file system or a bucket for these files: how do I decide?
items.ten_second: It depends on who reads the files. One instance: a volume. Many Linux instances: a file system. Code that calls an API: a bucket.
sixty_second: The short answer is: it depends on who reads the files, and how.
It works like this. A volume is block storage for a single instance.
A file system like Amazon EFS is shared. Many Linux instances mount it at the same time.
They can run in every Availability Zone of the Region. The code still reads and writes a normal directory.
A bucket in Amazon S3 stores objects. Your code reads and writes them through an API.
The thing to watch is the client. EFS is for Linux instances, not for Windows.
A bucket helps only if the code can use that API.
In your case, the report code writes to a directory, and it can't change this year.
So I'd mount one EFS file system on every instance.
Could the report code move to the S3 API next year?

key_points.point: Amazon EBS is block storage for a single EC2 instance or container; Amazon EFS is file storage; Amazon S3 is object storage.
accept: a volume attaches to one instance

key_points.point: File system storage fits applications that need shared read and write access across multiple EC2 instances or containers.
accept: many instances share one file system

key_points.point: EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones of the same Region can access one EFS file system at the same time.
accept: instances in every zone mount it

key_points.point: Object storage gives access to data through an API, so code that writes to a directory has to change before it can use Amazon S3.
accept: S3 needs API calls in the code
a bucket is not a directory

key_points.point: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported.
accept: EFS is for Linux, not Windows

key_points.point: Amazon EFS stores data within and across multiple Availability Zones and needs no changes to existing applications.

must_not_say.error: One EBS volume can be shared by all the web instances.
must_not_say.correct: Block storage is for a single EC2 instance or container. Many instances that share files need a file system such as Amazon EFS.

must_not_say.error: Amazon S3 works like a disk, with no code change.
must_not_say.correct: Amazon S3 is object storage that the code reaches through an API. Code that writes to a directory has to change to use it.

must_not_say.error: EFS works for Windows instances too.
must_not_say.correct: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported. Windows file shares belong on FSx for Windows File Server.

follow_ups.question: Do we need a mount target in every Availability Zone?
follow_ups.answer: You can create one mount target in each Availability Zone, and all instances in that zone share it. Create one in each zone where your instances run.

follow_ups.question: Does the file system fill up like a disk?
follow_ups.answer: No. You do not provision storage capacity for Amazon EFS. The file system grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files.

items.prompt: Our training data is 200 terabytes in S3, and our GPUs wait on data. Should we copy everything to EFS first?
items.persona: a machine learning founder in office hours
items.ten_second: No copy needed. Link FSx for Lustre to the bucket. The file list comes first, and file data loads when a job first reads it.
sixty_second: The short answer is no: link FSx for Lustre to the bucket instead.
Both are file systems that Linux instances mount. Lustre is built for speed, like machine learning.
It works like this. You link a Lustre file system to your S3 bucket.
The objects show up as files, so the training code reads a normal path.
A file's data loads from S3 the first time a job reads it.
Results can go back to S3.
The thing to watch is the deployment type.
A scratch file system doesn't replicate data. If a file server fails, that data is gone.
So the bucket stays your safe copy.
In your case, link the file system to the bucket you already have.
If a training run fails halfway, can your job read the data from S3 again?
skeleton: link to bucket, load on read

key_points.point: FSx for Lustre is for workloads where speed matters, such as machine learning and high performance computing (HPC).
accept: made for machine learning and HPC

key_points.point: A Lustre file system linked to an S3 bucket presents the objects as files and can write file system data back to S3.
accept: results go back to the bucket

key_points.point: An object's content is imported only when its file is first accessed, so the bucket is not copied before the job starts.
On a scratch file system data is not replicated and does not persist if a file server fails; on a persistent one data is replicated and failed servers are replaced.
SageMaker AI can use FSx for Lustre as an input data source, which removes the initial download step from Amazon S3.

key_points.point: AWS lists Linux as the client for FSx for Lustre.

must_not_say.correct: The content of an S3 object is imported only when its file is first accessed.

must_not_say.correct: Backups are not supported on scratch file systems, because they are designed for temporary storage.

follow_ups.question: What if the data has to stay on the file system for months?
follow_ups.answer: Use a persistent file system. Persistent file systems are for longer-term storage and throughput-focused workloads. Their data is replicated, and failed file servers are replaced.

follow_ups.question: Can our Windows laptops mount the Lustre file system?
follow_ups.answer: No. AWS lists Linux as the client for FSx for Lustre. Windows clients can use FSx for Windows File Server, FSx for NetApp ONTAP or FSx for OpenZFS.

items.prompt: Our EFS bill grows every month, and most of the files are old. What can we do without touching the application?
items.persona: a startup founder in office hours
items.ten_second: Turn on a lifecycle policy. EFS then moves unread files to cheaper storage classes, with no code change.
sixty_second: The short answer is: turn on a lifecycle policy on the file system.
It works like this. New files land in EFS Standard.
When a file goes unread for a set time, EFS moves it to Infrequent Access.
Infrequent Access costs much less to store.
Later it moves to Archive, for data read a few times a year.
It's a setting on the file system, not in your code. AWS gives you default times.
The thing to watch is reads. Reading a cold file adds a data access charge.
And by default, a cold file stays cold, even after someone reads it.
If old files get busy again, set the policy to move them back on first access.
In your case, I'd start with the defaults.
How often does anyone open a file that's older than a month?

key_points.point: EFS lifecycle management automatically transitions data between storage classes according to the lifecycle configuration of the file system.
accept: EFS moves the files for you
a setting on the file system

key_points.point: With a lifecycle policy at default settings, a file unread for 30 days moves to EFS IA, and one unread for 90 days to EFS Archive.
accept: unread files move to IA, then to Archive

key_points.point: EFS IA offers up to 95% lower cost than EFS Standard for infrequently accessed data.
accept: IA costs much less to store

key_points.point: Reading files in IA or Archive adds data access charges, and by default files stay in IA or Archive after they are read.
accept: reads of cold files cost extra
cold files do not move back by themselves

key_points.point: Set Transition into Standard to move files back on first access when the fastest latency matters.
accept: move them back on first access

key_points.point: EFS Archive has a minimum storage duration of 90 days, and IA and Archive bill each file as at least 128 KiB.
accept: tiny files cost more in IA
Archive keeps a file for a minimum time

must_not_say.error: The files move back to Standard by themselves when someone opens them.
must_not_say.correct: By default, files stay in IA or Archive when they are read. Set Transition into Standard to move them back on first access.

must_not_say.error: Cold storage is free to read.
must_not_say.correct: You are billed data access charges when files in IA or Archive are read.

must_not_say.error: You have to change the application to use Infrequent Access.
must_not_say.correct: Lifecycle management transitions data between storage classes according to the lifecycle configuration of the file system.

follow_ups.question: Which class fits files that people open a few times a year?
follow_ups.answer: EFS Archive. AWS designs EFS IA for data accessed a few times a quarter, and EFS Archive for data accessed a few times a year or less.

follow_ups.question: Does Archive change anything about our throughput mode?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. EFS Archive is supported on file systems with Elastic throughput. While the file system has a lifecycle policy that moves data to Archive, you cannot change the throughput mode to Bursting or Provisioned.
